title: Take a pause without closing the conversation
summary: Say that you need time to think, then come back to the conversation.

points.title: Stonewalling is withdrawing
sentences: Stonewalling is one of the four horsemen.
Flooded by emotion, a person withdraws from the conversation.
They go quiet, change the subject or leave the room.

points.title: It leaves the problem open
sentences: The other person feels ignored or rejected.
Nothing gets resolved, so the problem stays open.

points.title: Take a time-out instead
sentences: Say that you need time to think.
Then come back to the conversation.
The other person knows you haven't abandoned them.
example: For example, Roxanne tends to pull back when someone upsets her.
Now she says, "I need time to think. Can we talk tomorrow morning?"
The next morning, she comes back to the conversation.
outline: Say you need time to think
points.exampleOutline: Example. Roxanne asks for time, then comes back the next morning.

quiz.prompt: In a tense meeting, Michel feels his anger rising. How can he take a time-out rather than stonewall?

options.text: Stare at his screen without answering until the meeting ends
options.feedback: That's stonewalling. He withdraws without a word, and the others feel ignored.

options.text: Say he needs a few minutes, then come back to the discussion
options.feedback: He says he needs a pause and comes back.

options.text: Leave the room without a word to calm down
options.feedback: Calming down helps. Without saying so, the others may feel abandoned.

options.text: Change the subject to ease the tension
options.feedback: Changing the subject is stonewalling. The problem stays open.

quiz.prompt: What makes a pause a time-out rather than stonewalling?

options.feedback: Length isn't the test. A short silence with no word is still stonewalling.
Staring at a screen in the room is stonewalling too.

options.text: You say you need time, then come back
options.feedback: Saying so and coming back is what makes it a time-out.
